content.overview: Biosecurity starts with understanding how pests and plant pathogens can move through people, tools, media, water, containers, carts, plant material and work zones.

vocabulary.definition: Practices that reduce the introduction and spread of pests and plant pathogens.
A person, tool, material, organism or process that can move contamination between locations.
A movement sequence intended to reduce transfer from higher-risk areas into cleaner areas.

sections.title: Contamination has many routes
sections.body: Greenhouse disease sources can include plant debris, contaminated soil or media, tools, hose ends, containers, carts, water, incoming plants and worker movement. Clean material can be recontaminated when it contacts dirty surfaces or implements.

sections.title: Respect movement controls
sections.body: Facilities may use clean, general, quarantine or restricted zones. Whatever the naming system, workers follow the specified movement direction, tool/PPE change rules and sanitation steps rather than carrying material backward across a biosecurity boundary.

workedExamples: A hose nozzle that falls onto a dirty floor is treated according to the sanitation procedure before reuse.
A cart leaving quarantine is cleaned and released under the defined process before entering propagation.
commonMistakes: Assuming contamination only moves on visibly diseased plants.
Moving tools between rooms without following zone-specific rules.
content.practicalApplication: Map contamination routes on a mock facility plan and select the safest worker, tool and cart movement sequence using supplied zone rules.
content.summary: People, tools, water, media, containers and plants can all move contamination. Zone discipline and controlled movement are core Technician I behaviors.

blocks.title: Think in pathways, not appearances
blocks.body: A healthy-looking plant or apparently clean cart can still participate in a contamination route. The useful question is not only whether something looks dirty; it is how workers, tools, hose ends, containers, media, water, debris, and incoming plant material could move risk from one area to another.

blocks.alt: Cultivation facility pathway diagram showing a cleaner or sensitive zone, a controlled transition boundary, and a higher-risk or unresolved zone connected by workers, tools, carts, hose ends, incoming materials, and waste movement. It emphasizes controlled sanitation before crossing and avoiding unnecessary backward travel.
blocks.caption: Follow the pathway: clean status can be lost when an item re-enters an uncontrolled route.

items.title: Identify zone status
items.body: Use the facility's actual zone names and current procedure rather than inventing a universal label.

items.title: Plan direction
items.body: When the site uses clean-to-higher-risk sequencing, complete cleaner or more sensitive work before higher-risk work to reduce avoidable backward travel.

items.title: Control people and PPE
items.body: Follow clothing, glove, footwear, hand-hygiene, or other transition rules specified by the site.

items.title: Control tools and carts
items.body: Keep room-specific tools assigned where required and use the approved sanitation/release process for shared equipment.

items.title: Control material and waste
items.body: Preserve plant/material status and remove debris through the defined route instead of carrying it through cleaner areas.

left.label: Controlled pathway
left.body: A cart used in quarantine follows the approved cleaning/disinfection and release process before entering a cleaner or more sensitive area.

right.label: Appearance-based shortcut
right.body: A worker wipes the one visibly dirty spot on the cart and assumes the entire cart is safe to move between zones.

blocks.title: Quarantine cart urgently needed in propagation
blocks.setting: A cart has just been used in a quarantine area. Propagation needs the cart immediately, and no visible plant debris remains on the top shelf.
blocks.prompt: What should determine whether the cart crosses into propagation?
options: The approved cleaning/disinfection and release workflow for crossing the boundary
Whether the plants in quarantine looked healthy
blocks.answer: The approved cleaning/disinfection and release workflow for crossing the boundary.
blocks.feedback: Biosecurity controls are based on pathways and defined status, not only visible dirt or crop appearance. Urgency does not erase the cross-zone route.

blocks.title: Draw the contamination routes
blocks.instructions: On a supplied facility map, draw the possible routes created by technician travel, shared tools, carts, irrigation hose ends, incoming plants, and waste/debris removal. Then redesign the work sequence to reduce unnecessary cross-zone travel.
prompts: Mark every point where a person crosses a zone boundary.
Identify shared objects that could connect two areas.
Identify what must be cleaned, changed, contained, or verified before crossing.
Choose a work order that reduces avoidable backward travel.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Biosecurity is a movement-control problem as much as a cleaning problem. A technician protects cleaner areas by recognizing routes, following zone transitions, and preventing workers or objects from reconnecting a higher-risk pathway.
